A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HUMANVBENCH and contain complete main texts and supplementary material. Their text, tables, figures, and equation support comparison, including matching content moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original model and human evaluations, speaker-emotion experiments, class-wise analyses, and measurements of question-generation quality.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and question-generation measurements, plus timestamp experiments, modality ablations, and emotion-error analyses.

M1.justification: New Section 3.4 adds post-processing that tests models without visual input and removes frequently answerable questions to reduce answer leakage. The two underlying annotation and QA-generation pipelines remain substantially unchanged; face/body tracking details clarified in the main text were already documented in v1's appendix.

E1.justification: v2 removes the MELD-derived, seven-class Emotion Recognition in Conversation task, including its dialogue-history inputs and 210-question evaluation. This eliminates a distinct dataset and contextual emotion-understanding scenario, reducing coverage from 17 to 16 tasks. Stale MELD references remain in Section 12.3, but the task's definitions, construction procedure, and results are removed.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from 16 to 22 models, adding VideoLLaMA3, InternVL2/2.5, Qwen-VL2/2.5, and LLaVA-Video. Previously listed visual-only models also enter the speech-visual comparisons. Table 2 changes its speaker-emotion comparator roster, and new Table 5 compares visual-only and audio-visual VideoLLaMA2 variants.

E3.justification: Retained tasks have revised sample counts, including ER from 167 to 96 and AST from 70 to 100, alongside the new leakage-screening procedure. Table 1 changes VILA's reported frame count from 4 to 6 and Video-LLaMA2.1's from 16 to 8. New experiments introduce timestamp-augmented prompts and audio-plus-visual versus visual-only controls; these are distinct from the original evaluation settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds timestamp-inclusion experiments for ATD, AST, and TSA, VideoLLaMA2 modality ablations, Gemini emotion-error categories, and model-specific responses in the qualitative examples. It revises the speaking-subset evaluation while removing v1's Section 4.4 class-wise emotion and polarity analysis.

E5.justification: Five test runs with different random seeds and averaging were already reported in v1's Appendix Section 7. v2 states this practice in the Table 1 caption. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, dispersion estimates, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Many benchmark and speaker-subset scores are replaced, and new models, timestamp tests, modality ablations, and error categories add substantial results. For example, Gemini's ER accuracy changes from 67.1% to 57.3%, but ER's sample count also changes, so this is not a same-setting decline. ERC and class-wise emotion results disappear, while the question-generation effectiveness results are retained.

T1.justification: The face-to-body bounding-box selection expression, Equation 1, and its mathematical explanation are unchanged between v1's Appendix Section 9 and v2's Section 11. No new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations appear.

C1.justification: The abstract changes the claimed scope from 17 to 16 tasks and from 16 to 22 evaluated models, and shifts its emphasized weaknesses from cross-modal and temporal alignment to cross-modal understanding and emotion perception. The central contributions—a human-centric benchmark and two reusable automated construction pipelines—remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises interpretations of open-source versus proprietary performance and adds explanations involving partial lip-reading ability, ineffective use of audio, and explicit timestamp cues. It removes the class-wise emotion-bias discussion and the suggestion that audio mitigates speaker-emotion degradation. The appendix also newly states the benchmark's applicability to videos lasting at most 10 seconds.

D1.justification: v2 adds model sizes, decoding settings, memory usage, and runtimes for the new models, and revises existing runtime reports in Table 6. It newly discloses approximately three minutes of annotation per question, ten workdays in total, and 4.7 hours of video. Most operator settings, construction prompts, evaluation hardware, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including AuroraCap, MovieChat+, Data-Juicer 2.0, an answer-leakage evaluation study, and newer model papers, while removing the MELD reference. Its substantive positioning against HERM, HumanBench, and ActivityNet-QA remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Numerous paragraphs in Sections 3.1–3.3 are rewritten and condensed, particularly the annotation and QA-generation explanations. The results narrative is reorganized into vision-only and speech-visual subsections, and the appendix places statistics and modality analysis before evaluation implementation details. These changes substantially revise the exposition beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains model rows and loses the ERC column, Table 2 is regrouped, and Figure 4 adds model responses and replaces one example. v2 adds error-analysis, timestamp, and modality tables and a dataset-statistics figure, while removing the emotion radar plots and ERC example. The question-generation chart and final annotation example are retained with changed numbering and placement.

improvement.justification: Leakage screening, broader model comparisons, and timestamp/modality controls strengthen the evaluation design and diagnostic evidence. However, v2 removes conversation-emotion coverage and introduces numerical inconsistencies affecting interpretation: GPT-4o's listed emotion scores average 45.95%, not Table 1's 40.1%, and Table 4 marks Chat-UniVi's ATD change from 19.8 to 17.5 as an increase. These material reporting harms coexist with useful additions, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
